d1-1.ev: The 9th Armored captures the railway bridge intact, putting the first Americans across the Rhine.

q.t: What happened to the Ludendorff Bridge ten days after its capture?
o: It was blown by the Germans
q.x: Captured intact on 7 March, it put the first Americans across the Rhine and collapsed ten days later; its towers now hold the Peace Museum.

d1-1.rem: The surviving towers of the bridge that first put Americans across the Rhine now hold a Peace Museum.
d1-1.st: On 7 March 1945 the 9th Armored captured the Ludendorff railway bridge at Remagen intact, putting the first Americans across the Rhine. The bridge collapsed ten days later. Back at Mourmelon, Easy Company's veterans watched the Rhine crossings on the newsreels and wondered whether they would jump again. Today the surviving towers hold the Peace Museum, and the river's width shows the wall the Allies expected to fight for.

d1-2.ev: Men of the 506th visit the ruined city, its cathedral standing over the rubble.

q.t: What did 506th men see in Cologne in April 1945?
o: The cathedral standing amid the rubble
q.x: On passes, 506th men saw the cathedral standing over 90 % destruction and the Hohenzollern bridge in the river.

d1-2.rem: For most of the men, Cologne was the first German city they saw and the first proof of what the bombing had done.
d1-2.st: In April 1945 men of the 506th went into Cologne on passes. They found the cathedral standing amid 90 % destruction and the Hohenzollern bridge in the river. For most it was the first German city they had seen and the first proof of what the bombing had done. Today the cathedral tower gives the view the Americans had from the west bank, and the NS Documentation Centre nearby holds photographs of the ruins.

d1-3.ev: The 506th keeps its outpost line on the Rhine dike north of the town.

q.t: How had the war left Zons?
q.x: The medieval customs town was untouched by the war; the dike path north of it was the regiment's April 1945 outpost line.

d1-3.rem: Untouched by the war, Zons sits on the 506th's stretch of river; the dike path north was the regiment's outpost line.
d1-3.st: Zons, a medieval customs town between Cologne and Dormagen, lay on the 506th's stretch of the Rhine in April 1945 and came through the war untouched. The dike path north of the town was the regiment's outpost line, facing the Ruhr pocket across the water. Along this line the men kept watch and sent patrols across by boat. Today the dike path leads north toward Stürzelberg.

d1-4.ev: Easy mans outposts on the Rhine dike, facing the Ruhr pocket across the water.

q.t: How did Winters's patrols cross the Rhine here?
q.x: The 2nd Battalion HQ and Easy's outposts were here, facing the Ruhr pocket; patrols crossed the river by boat.

d1-4.rem: Easy's first sight of Germany was a country of white flags.
d1-4.st: In April 1945 the 2nd Battalion's headquarters and Easy Company's outposts stood in this village on the Rhine, facing the Ruhr pocket across the water. Winters' battalion HQ was in a village house on the river, and his patrols crossed here by boat. Easy's first sight of Germany was a country of white flags, and on 18 April the pocket gave up. Today from the dike the far bank, Germany's last industrial fortress, fills the view.

d2-1.ev: Easy is billeted in the town where Hitler wrote Mein Kampf, and hears of his death.

q.t: What did Hitler write in Landsberg's fortress prison?
o: Nothing; he was never held there
q.x: Hitler wrote Mein Kampf in the fortress prison in 1924; Easy was billeted in the town from 30 April 1945, when news came that he was dead.

d2-1.rem: On 30 April, in the town where Hitler had written Mein Kampf, the company learned he was dead in Berlin.
d2-1.st: Easy Company was billeted in Landsberg am Lech from 30 April 1945, in the town where Hitler had written Mein Kampf in the fortress prison in 1924. On 30 April the news came that he was dead in Berlin. Sink set up in the town, and the men were made to see the camp. Today the Lech weir and the painted old town are unchanged, with the prison on the hill above the Hauptplatz.

d2-2.ev: The Kaufering camps are revealed: of 30,000 Jews who passed through, 14,500 have died.
d2-2.rem: The only Kaufering camp that survives; its memorial stones honour the nations whose people died in the eleven camps.
d2-2.st: Kaufering VII is the only one of the eleven Kaufering camps that survives. 30,000 Jews passed through those camps building underground aircraft factories, and 14,500 of them died. Easy Company came upon this system at the end of April 1945, when it entered one of the sub-camps. Today the earth huts, the foundations and the memorial stones of the nations whose people died here remain; it is a place of remembrance first.

d2-3.ev: Easy Company enters a Kaufering sub-camp where the SS had burned the huts with the sick inside.
d2-3.rem: A memorial stone in the fields marks the camp usually identified as the one Easy Company entered in April 1945.
d2-3.st: This is the camp usually identified as the one Easy Company entered on 28–29 April 1945, Kaufering IV at Hurlach, a sub-camp of Dachau. Two days earlier the SS had set fire to the huts with the sick inside. Winters ordered food brought in, and Landsberg's citizens were marched out to bury the dead. Several Easy veterans later described it as one of their most disturbing experiences of the war. Today a memorial stone in the fields north of the village marks the site.

d2-4.ev: The 42nd and 45th Divisions liberate Dachau, the first camp and the model for the others.
d2-4.rem: The first camp and the model for all the others; the Kaufering camps were its sub-camps.
d2-4.st: Dachau was the first camp and the model for all the others, and the Kaufering camps were its sub-camps. It was liberated on 29 April 1945 by the 42nd and 45th Divisions, the same weekend Easy Company was at Landsberg and saw one of those sub-camps for itself. The memorial asks for time and attention. Today the site is free to enter, an audio guide is recommended, and a visit deserves the full time.

d3-1.ev: The 506th convoy passes through Munich, the 'capital of the movement', now a shell.

q.t: What stood on the site of the Documentation Centre?
o: The Brown House, the party's HQ
q.x: The centre stands on the site of the Brown House, the party's headquarters, and shows how Munich made the movement.

d3-1.rem: On the site of the party's headquarters, the centre explains how Munich made the movement, context for the Obersalzberg.
d3-1.st: The Munich Documentation Centre stands on the site of the Brown House, the party's headquarters. It explains how Munich made the movement and what the city later did with it. When Easy Company's convoy passed through on 3 May 1945, the 'capital of the movement' was a shell. The centre gives context for everything on the Obersalzberg. Today the Königsplatz outside, once the parade ground, is open to walk.

d3-2.ev: The 506th arrives on Hitler's mountain, and its men go down into the bunkers.

q.t: How does the museum describe the Obersalzberg's role?
q.x: The museum shows the Obersalzberg as the second seat of government, with a bunker system underneath, and the American arrival of May 1945.

d3-2.rem: Hitler's mountain served as a second seat of government; the 506th men went down into its bunkers.
d3-2.st: The museum on Hitler's mountain explains the Obersalzberg as the second seat of government, the bunker system beneath it and the American arrival of May 1945. Between 5 and 7 May, Easy men walked through the ruins of the Berghof and of Göring's and Bormann's houses and helped themselves to what was left. The centre, rebuilt and reopened in 2023, stands on that ground. Today the visitor can go down into the bunkers, as the 506th men did.

d3-3.ev: Easy men walk through the ruins of the Berghof and Göring's house.

q.t: What happened to most of the Obersalzberg's Nazi buildings?
q.x: Most were demolished in 1952 and the rest cleared later; the site is forested, with the Berghof terrace retaining wall still visible.

d3-3.rem: Of Hitler's house only foundations and the terrace retaining wall remain, now among the trees.
d3-3.st: The Berghof was bombed by the RAF on 25 April 1945 and burned by the SS. In early May Easy men walked through the ruins of Hitler's house, Göring's and Bormann's houses and the SS barracks, and Göring's wine cellar became legend. Most of it was demolished in 1952, the rest cleared later, and the ground is now forested. Today signed paths lead from the Dokumentation centre, and the Berghof terrace's retaining wall still stands in the trees.

d3-4.ev: The 506th enters Berchtesgaden and takes the Berchtesgadener Hof as regimental HQ.

q.t: Where did the 506th set up its headquarters in Berchtesgaden?
q.x: Sink took the Berchtesgadener Hof, the Nazi Party's grand hotel, as regimental HQ; it stood until 2006 and the plot is now a park.

d3-4.rem: VE Day, 8 May 1945, found the 506th here, where the war in Europe ended for Easy Company.
d3-4.st: The 506th entered Berchtesgaden on the afternoon of 5 May 1945. Sink took the Berchtesgadener Hof, the Nazi Party's grand hotel, as regimental HQ, and the men found its wine cellars, silver and Mercedes limousines. On 8 May the war in Europe ended with the regiment here, and Winters ordered that all troops would stand fast. The hotel was demolished in 2006. Today its plot near Haus der Berge is a park, and the Maximilianstrasse is worth walking.

d4-1.ev: Winters, Nixon, Welsh and Easy men reportedly go up to the tea-house on the Kehlstein.

q.t: Why did the Kehlsteinhaus survive the war?
q.x: The house survived because the RAF missed it; its terrace is traditionally identified as the setting of the famous Easy Company photograph, though this is disputed.

d4-1.rem: The famous photograph of Easy men on a terrace, traditionally placed here, shows the end of the company's war in one frame.
d4-1.st: The Kehlsteinhaus, 1,834 m up, was built as a tea-house for Hitler's 50th birthday and survived because the RAF missed it. Winters, Nixon, Welsh and Easy men are said to have gone up after 5 May 1945, though who got there first is disputed, as is whether they used the lift. A famous photograph of them is traditionally placed on its terrace, though the exact location is disputed. Today the terrace looks out to the Watzmann.

d4-2.ev: Men of the 506th swim and boat on the lake below the Watzmann.

q.t: What did the 506th do at the Königssee in May 1945?
q.x: In May 1945 the 506th swam and boated on the fjord-like lake below the Watzmann.

d4-2.rem: With the war ending, the lake below the Watzmann was where 506th men swam and boated.
d4-2.st: In May 1945, after the 506th reached Berchtesgaden, its men swam and went boating on the Königssee, the fjord-like lake below the Watzmann. For soldiers who had come through Normandy, Holland, Bastogne and Haguenau, the war in Europe was ending in scenes like this, with the lake as a place of rest. Today electric boats run to St Bartholomä, the echo trumpet still plays, and the lake offers a rest from the museums.

d4-3.ev: The 506th's column waits at a blown bridge while others reach Berchtesgaden first.

q.t: Who reached Berchtesgaden first while the 506th waited here?
o: The 3rd Infantry Division and the French
q.x: The column was held up at a blown bridge on 4 May while the US 3rd Infantry Division and the French 2nd Armoured got into the town first.

d4-3.rem: A demolished bridge here cost the 506th the race into Berchtesgaden; Sink was not pleased.
d4-3.st: On 4 May 1945 the 506th's column was held up at a demolished bridge on the road into the Berchtesgaden valley, near this spa town at the valley mouth. While it waited, the US 3rd Infantry Division and the French 2nd Armoured got into Berchtesgaden first, and Sink was not pleased. The regiment entered the town the following afternoon. Today the main road east toward the valley marks the axis of that advance.

d5-1.ev: The 506th makes Zell am See its occupation capital for the summer.

q.t: What did the men sail on the lake at Zell am See?
q.x: Zell am See was the 506th's occupation capital in the summer of 1945; the men swam in the lake and sailed Göring's yacht.

d5-1.rem: Men with 85 points went home from here, while the rest trained for the Pacific and waited.
d5-1.st: From 9 May 1945 the 506th moved over the border into the Austrian Salzburg province to disarm the German forces there, and Zell am See became the regiment's occupation capital for the summer. In June training for the Pacific began again; men with enough points went home, and the rest swam in the lake and sailed Göring's yacht. The regiment left Austria on 1 July. Today the Elisabeth promenade runs along the lake.

d5-2.ev: Col. Sink sets up the regimental HQ in the Grand Hotel on the lake.

q.t: Whose headquarters was in the Grand Hotel?
q.x: Sink's regimental HQ was in the Grand Hotel on the lake; the ballroom and terrace remain as the regiment knew them.

d5-2.rem: The ballroom and terrace are as the regiment knew them; that summer the whole valley was the regiment's.
d5-2.st: In May 1945 Sink set up the 506th's regimental headquarters in the Grand Hotel, on its promontory in the lake at Zell am See. From here the regiment ran its occupation of the valley through the summer, disarming German forces while training for the Pacific resumed. The ballroom and terrace are as the regiment knew them. Today it is still a hotel, and coffee on the terrace looks across to Thumersbach.

d5-3.ev: Easy is billeted in the village on occupation duty with the 2nd Battalion HQ.

q.t: Where is Sgt. Grant's shooting usually placed?
o: At a road-block on the valley road
q.x: The shooting is usually placed at a road-block on the valley road; the exact spot, like the company's billets, is not documented.

d5-3.rem: Easy's billets and the 2nd Battalion HQ were here in May–June 1945, on occupation duty at the foot of the Glockner range.
d5-3.st: From May to June 1945 Easy Company was billeted in Kaprun, at the foot of the Glockner range, with the 2nd Battalion HQ. Occupation duty meant road-blocks, collecting weapons and guarding the dam construction site with its slave-labour camp, along with swimming, hunting and drinking. The shooting of Sgt. Grant is usually placed at a road-block on the valley road, though the exact spot is not documented. Today the castle and church anchor a village grown around the ski trade.

d5-4.ev: The 506th guards the dam site, begun with forced and slave labour, and its DP camp.

q.t: Who was used to build the Kaprun dams from 1938?
o: Forced and slave labour from the camps
q.x: The project was begun in 1938 with forced and slave labour from the camps; the 506th guarded the site and its DP camp in 1945.

d5-4.rem: The dams were begun with forced and slave labour from the camps; a memorial at the dam remembers the forced labourers.
d5-4.st: The Kaprun hydro-electric project was begun in 1938 with forced and slave labour from the camps. In 1945 the 506th guarded the site and its DP camp as part of its occupation duty. The dams were finished after the war and became a symbol of Austrian reconstruction. Today a bus and an inclined lift climb to the dams, where a memorial to the forced labourers can be read and the exhibition 'Erlebniswelt Strom' is on show.

d5-5.ev: German units march into the valley to surrender their weapons to the 506th.

q.t: What happened to Sgt. Grant at Saalfelden?
o: A German surgeon saved his life
q.x: A German brain surgeon saved Sgt. Grant's life here, in the basin where German units came in to surrender.

d5-5.rem: Tens of thousands of German soldiers passed through this basin, ordered to stack their weapons and go home.
d5-5.st: In May 1945 German units marched into this wide valley to surrender to the 506th, and Winters supervised columns ordered to stack their weapons and go home. Tens of thousands of German soldiers were processed through the Saalfelden–Zell basin, though which formation and commander is not recorded in a primary source. Here too a German surgeon saved Sgt. Grant's life. Today the Steinernes Meer above the town forms the backdrop familiar from the surrender photographs.

dd-0.ev: American and Soviet troops meet on the Elbe and cut Germany in two.

q.t: What happened at Torgau?
q.x: At Torgau, on 25 April 1945, American and Soviet troops met and cut Germany in two.

dd-0.rem: The meeting at Torgau cut Germany in two.
dd-0.st: At Torgau on the Elbe, on 25 April 1945, American and Soviet troops met and cut Germany in two. In those same days the 101st was travelling south by truck and DUKW down the autobahn through Württemberg, past columns of surrendering Germans. The meeting on the river showed how little of the Reich was left. Today a memorial stands on the river, some four hours east of the route.

dd-1.ev: Hitler's end comes in Berlin as the Reich collapses.

q.t: What is on the Führerbunker site today?
o: A car park with an information board
q.x: The end of Hitler and of the Reich came here; the bunker site is now a car park with an information board.

dd-1.rem: Hitler died in Berlin on 30 April; Easy heard the news that day in Landsberg.
dd-1.st: Berlin saw the end of Hitler and of the Reich between 30 April and 2 May 1945. The news of his death reached Easy Company in its billets at Landsberg on 30 April. The site of the Führerbunker, where that ending played out, is now a car park with an information board. Today it lies far off the route, with the Topography of Terror nearby for those who make the journey.

dd-2.ev: The courtroom near the party's former rally ground hosts the trials of 1945–46.

q.t: Which two stories does Nuremberg tell?
o: The party rallies and the trials
q.x: Nuremberg holds the party's parade ground and the courtroom of the 1945–46 trials.

dd-2.rem: The same city holds the party's rally ground and the courtroom where the 1945–46 trials took place.
dd-2.st: Nuremberg was both the party's parade ground, the Zeppelinfeld, where the rallies were held, and the setting of the courtroom for the trials of 1945–46. It holds the rise and the reckoning of the regime whose mountain retreat Easy Company reached in May 1945. The Documentation Centre tells that story on the rally grounds. Today both sites lie on the road south.

dd-3.ev: The Austrian main camp is liberated the day Easy reaches Berchtesgaden.
dd-3.rem: The Austrian main camp was liberated on 5 May 1945, the day Easy reached Berchtesgaden.
dd-3.st: Mauthausen was the Austrian main camp. It was liberated on 5 May 1945, the same day Easy Company reached Berchtesgaden. A few weeks later the regiment was guarding the Kaprun dam site, built with forced and slave labour from the camps, a reminder of how far that system reached. Today the Mauthausen Memorial lies two hours east of Zell am See, and it is a place for quiet remembrance.
